structure.title: Synthesis, structure, and ionic conductivity of solid solution, $\text{Li}_{10+\delta}M_{1+\delta}P_{2-\delta}S_{12}$ (M = Si, Sn)
structure.text:
Satoshi Hori.<sup>a</sup> Kota Suzuki.<sup>a</sup> Masaaki Hiravama.<sup>a</sup> Yuki Kato.<sup>b</sup> Toshiya Saito,<sup>b</sup> Masao Yonemura<sup>c</sup> and Ryoji Kanno<sup>\*a</sup>

Received 1st July 2014, Accepted 18th August 2014

DOI: 10.1039/c4fd00143e

Solid solutions of the silicon and tin analogous phases of the superionic conductor  $Li_{10}MP_2S_{12}$  (M = Si, Sn) were synthesized by a conventional solid-state reaction in an evacuated silica tube at 823 K. The ranges of the solid solutions were determined to be  $0.20 < \delta < 0.43$  and  $-0.25 < \delta < -0.01$  in  $\text{Li}_{10+\delta}M_{1+\delta}P_{2-\delta}S_{12}$  (0.525  $\leq k \leq 0.60$  and 0.67  $\leq k \leq 0.75$  in  $\text{Li}_{4-k}M_{1-k}P_kS_4$ ) for the Si and Sn systems, respectively. The ionic conductivity of these systems varied as a function of the changing M ions: the Si and Sn systems showed lower conductivity than the Ge system,  $Li_{10+\delta}Ge_{1+\delta}P_{2-\delta}S_{12}$ . The conductivity change for different elements might be due to the lattice size and lithium content affecting the ionic conduction. The relationship between ionic conduction, structure, and lithium concentration is discussed based on the structural and electrochemical information for the silicon, germanium, and tin systems.

structure.title: Introduction
structure.text:
Solid lithium ionic conductors are of technological importance for future applications as solid electrolytes for all-solid-state batteries, which are expected to solve the safety issues in current lithium batteries by replacing flammable liquid electrolytes with solid electrolytes. The conditions required for high lithium ionic conductors for battery applications are considered to be as follows: (i) a high lithium ionic conductivity ( $\geq 1.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ S cm}^{-1}$ ) at room temperature with negligible electronic conduction, (ii) high ionic transport number, (iii) electrochemical stability, and (iv) low-cost elements.2 Recently, a lithium containing sulphide with a composition of Li<sub>10</sub>GeP<sub>2</sub>S<sub>12</sub> (LGPS) was reported to exhibit a wide electrochemical window of up to 5 V and an extremely

<sup>&</sup>lt;sup>a</sup>Department of Electronic Chemistry, Tokyo Institute of Technology, 4259 Nagatsuta-cho, Midori-ku, Yokohama, 226-8502, Japan. E-mail: kanno@echem.titech.ac.jp; Fax: +81 045 924 5570

<sup>&</sup>lt;sup>b</sup>Battery Research Division, Higashifuji Technical Center, Toyota Motor Corporation 1200 Mishuku, Susono, Shizuoka 410-1193, Japan

<sup>&</sup>lt;sup>e</sup>Neutron Science Laboratory (KENS), Institute of Materials Structure Science, High Energy Accelerator Research Organization (KEK), 1-1 Oho, Tsukuba, Ibaraki 305-0801, Japan

high conductivity value of  $1.2 \times 10^{-2}$  S cm<sup>-1</sup>, which almost equals the conductivity values of liquid electrolytes.<sup>3</sup> The discovery of LGPS opened the door to a new era of materials research, targeting new crystalline solid electrolytes with the same structure as LGPS. Its structure, shown in Fig. 1, consists of one-dimensional chains formed by LiS<sub>6</sub> octahedra and  $(Ge_{0.5}/P_{0.5})S_4$  tetrahedra, which are connected by a common edge, and these chains are connected at a corner with PS<sub>4</sub> tetrahedra.

The search for new LGPS-type compounds is of practical importance for battery applications, because the use of rare and expensive germanium increases the cost of the electrolyte. The substitution of  $\mathrm{Ge^{4^+}}$  with  $\mathrm{Sn^{4^+}}$  yields  $\mathrm{Li_{10}SnP_2S_{12}}$ , which shows a lower conductivity value of  $4.0 \times 10^{-3}$  S cm<sup>-1</sup> at room temperature; the  $\mathrm{Si^{4^+}}$ -substituted material,  $\mathrm{Li_{11}Si_2PS_{12}}$ , was also synthesized under high-pressure conditions. On the other hand, the ionic conduction mechanism of these phases was studied based on information on the crystal structures, dynamics of ionic motion, and theoretical analysis. In particular,  $\mathrm{Li_{10}SiP_2S_{12}}$  has been predicted to have a higher bulk conductivity value than the LGPS phase, from first principle calculations. Materials synthesis and an understanding of the conduction mechanism in these LGPS-type analogous phases are still issues to be considered.

In the present study, the LGPS-related phases,  $\operatorname{Li}_{10+\delta}M_{1+\delta}P_{2-\delta}S_{12}$  where  $M=\operatorname{Si}$  and Sn, were synthesized by a conventional solid-state reaction in a sealed and evacuated silica tube. The ranges of the solid solutions were determined, and the conductivity and electrochemical stabilities were clarified. The relationships between ionic conduction, metal ions, lithium content, lattice volume, and local environment of lithium along the conduction pathway were studied on the basis of the crystal structures and conductivities of these solid solutions. The conduction mechanism is discussed for the  $\operatorname{Li}_{10+\delta}M_{1+\delta}P_{2-\delta}S_{12}$  ( $M=\operatorname{Si}$ , Ge, Sn) systems with the LGPS-type structure in order to develop further materials design of these solid lithium ion conductors.

![](page_1_Figure_6.jpeg)

Fig. 1 Framework structure of the  $Li_{10}GeP_2S_{12}$  (LGPS) crystal. Hatched blue octahedra, dark purple tetrahedra, and light green tetrahedra represent LiS<sub>6</sub>, (Ge<sub>0.5</sub>/P<sub>0.5</sub>)S<sub>4</sub>, and PS<sub>4</sub>. The dotted lines represent the unit cell. Lithium atoms participating in ionic conduction are not drawn for simplicity.

nodes.title: Structure, Challenges, and Mechanism Studies of LGPS Analogs
nodes.text: Its structure, shown in Fig. 1, consists of one-dimensional chains formed by LiS<sub>6</sub> octahedra and  $(Ge_{0.5}/P_{0.5})S_4$  tetrahedra, which are connected by a common edge, and these chains are connected at a corner with PS<sub>4</sub> tetrahedra. The search for new LGPS-type compounds is of practical importance for battery applications, because the use of rare and expensive germanium increases the cost of the electrolyte. The substitution of  $\mathrm{Ge^{4^+}}$  with  $\mathrm{Sn^{4^+}}$  yields  $\mathrm{Li_{10}SnP_2S_{12}}$ , which shows a lower conductivity value of  $4.0 \times 10^{-3}$  S cm<sup>-1</sup> at room temperature; the  $\mathrm{Si^{4^+}}$ -substituted material,  $\mathrm{Li_{11}Si_2PS_{12}}$ , was also synthesized under high-pressure conditions. On the other hand, the ionic conduction mechanism of these phases was studied based on information on the crystal structures, dynamics of ionic motion, and theoretical analysis. In particular,  $\mathrm{Li_{10}SiP_2S_{12}}$  has been predicted to have a higher bulk conductivity value than the LGPS phase, from first principle calculations. Materials synthesis and an understanding of the conduction mechanism in these LGPS-type analogous phases are still issues to be considered.

nodes.title: Aims and Scope of the Current Research
nodes.text: In the present study, the LGPS-related phases,  $\operatorname{Li}_{10+\delta}M_{1+\delta}P_{2-\delta}S_{12}$  where  $M=\operatorname{Si}$  and Sn, were synthesized by a conventional solid-state reaction in a sealed and evacuated silica tube. The ranges of the solid solutions were determined, and the conductivity and electrochemical stabilities were clarified. The relationships between ionic conduction, metal ions, lithium content, lattice volume, and local environment of lithium along the conduction pathway were studied on the basis of the crystal structures and conductivities of these solid solutions. The conduction mechanism is discussed for the  $\operatorname{Li}_{10+\delta}M_{1+\delta}P_{2-\delta}S_{12}$  ( $M=\operatorname{Si}$ , Ge, Sn) systems with the LGPS-type structure in order to develop further materials design of these solid lithium ion conductors.

structure.title: **Experimental**
structure.text:
The starting materials in this work were Li<sub>2</sub>S (Idemitsu Kosan, >99.9% purity), P<sub>2</sub>S<sub>5</sub> (Aldrich, >99.9% purity), SiS<sub>2</sub> (Mitsuwa Chemical, >99% purity), and SnS<sub>2</sub> (Kojundo Chemical Laboratory, >99% purity). These were weighed in appropriate molar ratios in an Ar-filled glove box, and mixed by planetary ball-milling for 40 h. The specimens were then pressed into pellets, sealed in a carbon-coated quartz tube at 10 Pa, and heated at a reaction temperature of 823 K for 3 days. After heating, the tube was slowly cooled to room temperature. The synthesized materials were characterized by an X-ray diffractometer (Rigaku SmartLab) with CuKα radiation. Diffraction data were collected at each 0.01° step width over the  $2\theta$  range from  $10^{\circ}$  to  $35^{\circ}$ . Synchrotron X-ray diffraction data for structural analysis were obtained using a high-flux synchrotron X-ray source at the BL19B2 beamline at SPring-8, operating at room temperature with a wavelength of 0.5 Å or 0.6 Å. A Debye-Scherrer diffraction camera was used for the measurements, and the specimens were sealed under vacuum in a Lindemann glass capillary (about 0.5 mm in diameter). The structural and profile parameters were refined by Rietveld analysis with the refinement program RIETAN-FP. 10 Neutron diffraction data were obtained using a special environmental neutron powder diffractometer (SPICA) installed on the BL09 beamline at the Japan Proton Accelerator Research Complex in Tokai, Japan. The specimen was sealed in a vanadium cell (about 6 mm diameter) with an indium ring. Rietveld refinement of the data was performed using the Z-Rietveld program.11

The electrochemical window of the solid electrolyte (SE) was evaluated by cyclic voltammetry. An Au electrode and a lithium electrode were used as a working, and a counter and reference electrode, respectively. The asymmetric Li/SE/Au cell was examined with a scan rate of 1 mV s<sup>-1</sup> and scan range between -0.5 V and 5 V using a Solartron 1287 electrochemical interface. Ionic conductivity was measured by the ac impedance method in an Ar gas flow over a 253 K  $\leq T \leq$  373 K temperature range with applied frequencies in the range between 100 Hz and 15 MHz using a Solartron 1260 frequency response analyser. The sample was pressed into a pellet (diameter 11–12 mm; thickness 1–2 mm) and heated at 823 K in vacuum. The pellet was then coated with Au to form electrodes.

structure.title: Materials synthesis
structure.text: Solid solutions of the germanium system,  $\text{Li}_{10+\delta}\text{Ge}_{1+\delta}\text{P}_{2-\delta}\text{S}_{12}$ , were synthesized with a composition range of  $0 \le \delta \le 0.35$  at 823 K by the conventional solid-state reaction. Similar solid solutions can be expected for silicon- and tin-based LGPS-type phases. As superionic conducting phases of the LGPS-type structure exist in the binary  $\text{Li}_4M\text{S}_4-\text{Li}_3\text{PS}_4$  system (M=Si,Ge,Sn), the composition of the phase could be described by the formula,  $\text{Li}_{4-k}M_{1-k}P_k\text{S}_4$ , where the ratio, 1-k:k, corresponds to the molar ratio of  $M^{4+}:\text{P}^{5+}$ . Based on the original LGPS phase, the solid solution is described by  $\text{Li}_{10+\delta}M_{1+\delta}P_{2-\delta}\text{S}_{12}$ , where the original composition of  $\text{Li}_{10}\text{GeP}_2\text{S}_{12}$  ( $\delta=0.0$  in  $\text{Li}_{10+\delta}M_{1+\delta}P_{2-\delta}\text{S}_{12}$ ) corresponds to k=0.67 in  $\text{Li}_{4-k}M_{1-k}P_k\text{S}_4$ . In the present study, the compositions of the solid solutions were described mainly by the k value in  $\text{Li}_{4-k}M_{1-k}P_k\text{S}_4$ .

structure.title: Silicon system
structure.text: A previous material search on the pseudo binary Li4SiS4-Li3PS4 system indicated the existence of the lithium conducting phase, Li3.4Si0.4P0.6S4, which was regarded as a member of the thio-LISICON family with a conductivity value of $6.4 \times 10^{-4}$ S cm-1 at room temperature.13 The Li3.4Si0.4P0.6S4 phase is composed of a three-dimensional framework structure formed by isolated PS4 tetrahedral units, which is different from the LGPS-type structure. The solid-state synthesis of the binary system in this study confirmed the existence of the LGPS-type phase with the nominal composition of $Li_{3,45}Si_{0,45}P_{0,55}S_4$ and $Li_{10,35}Si_{1,35}P_{1,65}S_{12}$ (k = 0.55 in $\text{Li}_{4-k}\text{Si}_{1-k}\text{P}_k\text{S}_4$ and $\delta = 0.35$ in $\text{Li}_{10+\delta}\text{Si}_{1+\delta}\text{P}_{2-\delta}\text{S}_{12}$ , which was close to that of the thio-LISICON phase, $\text{Li}_{3.4}\text{Si}_{0.4}\text{P}_{0.6}\text{S}_4$ (k = 0.6 in $\text{Li}_{4-k}\text{Si}_{1-k}\text{P}_k\text{S}_4$ ). Fig. 2(a) shows synchrotron X-ray diffraction patterns of Li3,45Si0,45P0,55S4. All the diffraction peaks were indexed by the same space group as LGPS, P42/nmc (137), although small diffraction peaks indexed by Li3PO4, which was present in the raw starting materials, were also observed. The amount of the impurity phase was calculated to be ca. 3.8 wt% by Rietveld refinements. The refined lattice parameters, a = 8.67088(8) Å and c = 12.53955(19) Å, are smaller than those of LGPS (a = 8.71771(5) Å and c = 12.63452(10) Å), indicating that $Ge^{4+}$ (ionic radii r = 0.39 Å) ions are substituted by $Si^{4+}$ (r = 0.26 Å). The structure parameters were refined by Rietveld analysis using neutron diffraction data at room temperature. The composition was fixed to Li3,45Si0,45P0,55S4 and multiphase models were employed for the small amount of impurity phase throughout the refinements. The structure model of the LGPS was used for the initial refinement. Four lithium sites reported recently, $^{9,12}$ the 16h, 4d, 8f, and 4c sites, were employed as initial positions. Initial atomic positions for other elements were as follows: S at 8g sites, P at 2b sites and 4d sites, and Si at 4d sites. Isotropic Debye-Waller factors were used for all atoms at the initial stage of the refinements, and then anisotropic Debye-Waller factors were applied to the four Li atoms. Several structure models were examined to determine the Si position; the model of Si in the 4d site provided better fitting results than the structure model with partial disordering of Si in the 2b site. Lithium was found to be distributed over four sites: Li(1) on the 16h site (site occupation parameter, g = 0.488(4)), Li(2) on the 4d site (g = 1.0), Li(3) on the 8f site (g = 0.716(8)), and Li(4) on the 4c site (g = 0.791(3)). Bragg positions for secondary Li3PO4 phases are represented by the lower vertical marks. nodes.title: Background and Synthesis
nodes.text: A previous material search on the pseudo binary Li<sub>4</sub>SiS<sub>4</sub>-Li<sub>3</sub>PS<sub>4</sub> system indicated the existence of the lithium conducting phase, Li<sub>3.4</sub>Si<sub>0.4</sub>P<sub>0.6</sub>S<sub>4</sub>, which was regarded as a member of the thio-LISICON family with a conductivity value of  $6.4 \times 10^{-4}$  S cm<sup>-1</sup> at room temperature.<sup>13</sup> The Li<sub>3.4</sub>Si<sub>0.4</sub>P<sub>0.6</sub>S<sub>4</sub> phase is composed of a three-dimensional framework structure formed by isolated PS4 tetrahedral units, which is different from the LGPS-type structure. The solid-state synthesis of the binary system in this study confirmed the existence of the LGPS-type phase with the nominal composition of  $Li_{3,45}Si_{0,45}P_{0,55}S_4$  and  $Li_{10,35}Si_{1,35}P_{1,65}S_{12}$  (k = 0.55 in  $\text{Li}_{4-k}\text{Si}_{1-k}\text{P}_k\text{S}_4$  and  $\delta = 0.35$  in  $\text{Li}_{10+\delta}\text{Si}_{1+\delta}\text{P}_{2-\delta}\text{S}_{12}$ , which was close to that of the thio-LISICON phase,  $\text{Li}_{3.4}\text{Si}_{0.4}\text{P}_{0.6}\text{S}_4$  (k = 0.6 in  $\text{Li}_{4-k}\text{Si}_{1-k}\text{P}_k\text{S}_4$ ).

nodes.title: Synchrotron X-ray Diffraction and Initial Characterization
nodes.text: Fig. 2(a) shows synchrotron X-ray diffraction patterns of Li<sub>3,45</sub>Si<sub>0,45</sub>P<sub>0,55</sub>S<sub>4</sub>. All the diffraction peaks were indexed by the same space group as LGPS, P42/nmc (137), although small diffraction peaks indexed by Li<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>, which was present in the raw starting materials, were also observed. The amount of the impurity phase was calculated to be ca. 3.8 wt% by Rietveld refinements. The refined lattice parameters, a = 8.67088(8) Å and c = 12.53955(19) Å, are smaller than those of LGPS (a = 8.71771(5) Å and c = 12.63452(10) Å), indicating that  $Ge^{4+}$  (ionic radii r = 0.39 Å) ions are substituted by  $Si^{4+}$  (r = 0.26 Å).

nodes.title: Neutron Rietveld Refinement: Methodology and Lithium Distribution
nodes.text: The structure parameters were refined by Rietveld analysis using neutron diffraction data at room temperature. The composition was fixed to Li<sub>3,45</sub>Si<sub>0,45</sub>P<sub>0,55</sub>S<sub>4</sub> and multiphase models were employed for the small amount of impurity phase throughout the refinements. The structure model of the LGPS was used for the initial refinement. Four lithium sites reported recently,  $^{9,12}$  the 16h, 4d, 8f, and 4c sites, were employed as initial positions. Initial atomic positions for other elements were as follows: S at 8g sites, P at 2b sites and 4d sites, and Si at 4d sites. Isotropic Debye-Waller factors were used for all atoms at the initial stage of the refinements, and then anisotropic Debye-Waller factors were applied to the four Li atoms. Several structure models were examined to determine the Si position; the model of Si in the 4d site provided better fitting results than the structure model with partial disordering of Si in the 2b site. Lithium was found to be distributed over four sites: Li(1) on the 16h site (site occupation parameter, g = 0.488(4)), Li(2) on the 4d site (g = 1.0), Li(3) on the 8f site (g = 0.716(8)), and Li(4) on the 4c site (g = 0.791(3)). structure.title: Silicon solid-solution system
structure.text:
Solid solutions were synthesized according to the composition  $\text{Li}_{4-k}\text{Si}_{1-k}P_kS_4$ . Fig. 3(a) shows X-ray diffraction patterns for the samples with  $0.45 \le k \le 0.65$  in  $\text{Li}_{4-k}\text{Si}_{1-k}P_kS_4$ , together with the diffraction data for  $\text{Li}_4\text{SiS}_4$  and  $\beta\text{-Li}_3\text{PS}_4$ ,  $^{13,14}$  which corresponds to the composition, k=0 and 1.0, respectively. The figure shows select diffraction lines, indicating a continuous peak shift in the composition range of  $0.525 \le k \le 0.60$ . The samples for k=0.45 and 0.50 show additional diffraction lines due to the phase with a similar structure to  $\text{Li}_4\text{SiS}_4$ . On the other hand, the sample with k=0.65 shows diffraction lines due to the presence of  $\beta\text{-Li}_3\text{PS}_4$ . The lattice parameters, a and c, and volume V were calculated based on the LGPS-type structure. Fig. 3(b) shows the lattice parameters and volume of  $\text{Li}_{4-k}\text{Si}_{1-k}P_kS_4$ . A continuous decrease in the lattice parameters was observed with the variation of k from 0.525 to 0.60, which corresponds to the range of the solid solution.

The decrease in the lattice parameter is due to a decrease in the silicon content (Si<sup>4+</sup>: r = 0.26 Å; P<sup>5+</sup>: r = 0.17 Å), and also due to a decrease in the lithium content in the structure.

structure.title: Tin solid-solution system
structure.text:
The solid solution of the Sn-substituted system was synthesized at 823 K by the solid-state reaction based on the composition,  $0.50 \le k \le 0.75$  in  $\text{Li}_{4-k}\text{Sn}_{1-k}P_kS_4$ 

![](page_5_Figure_3.jpeg)

Fig. 3 (a) XRD patterns (left) and peak shifts (right) for the sample,  $\text{Li}_{4-k}\text{Si}_{1-k}\text{P}_k\text{S}_4$  (0.45  $\leq k$  $\leq$  0.65). XRD patterns for Li<sub>4</sub>SiS<sub>4</sub> and  $\beta$ -Li<sub>3</sub>PS<sub>4</sub> are also shown. (b) Composition dependence of the lattice parameters in LGPS-type phase with k in  $\text{Li}_{4-k}\text{Si}_{1-k}\text{P}_k\text{S}_4$ .

 $(-0.25 \le \delta \le 0.50 \text{ in } \text{Li}_{10+\delta}\text{Sn}_{1+\delta}\text{P}_{2-\delta}\text{S}_{12})$ , which is near the original LGPS composition of Li<sub>10</sub>SnP<sub>2</sub>S<sub>12</sub>. Fig. 4(a) shows X-ray diffraction patterns for the sample with  $\text{Li}_{4-k}\text{Sn}_{1-k}\text{P}_k\text{S}_4$  (0.50  $\leq k \leq$  0.75). The mono-phasic region of the LGPS-type structure was obtained near the composition k = 0.73, and the samples with the compositions  $0.50 \le k \le 0.65$  and k = 0.75 showed additional diffraction peaks due to the Li<sub>4</sub>SnS<sub>4</sub>-type phase and the β-Li<sub>3</sub>PS<sub>4</sub>-type phase, respectively. <sup>14,15</sup> On the other hand, the sample with  $0.67 \le k \le 0.72$  showed diffraction peaks from a small amount of impurity phases, and the samples with k = 0.73 and 0.74 were found to be mono-phasic in character. Fig. 4(b) shows the lattice parameters and volume of the  $Li_{4-k}Sn_{1-k}P_kS_4$  phase obtained in the present study. The lattice parameters decreased from k = 0.67 to 0.75, indicating the formation of the solid solution. The decrease in the lattice parameter is due to a decrease in the amount of  $\operatorname{Sn}^{4+}$  ions that have a larger ionic radius (r = 0.55 Å)than the  $P^{5+}$  ion (r = 0.17 Å), and also due to a decrease in the lithium content in the structure.

The mono-phasic region of the LGPS-type structure was obtained near the composition k = 0.73, and the samples with the compositions  $0.50 \le k \le 0.65$  and k = 0.75 showed additional diffraction peaks due to the Li<sub>4</sub>SnS<sub>4</sub>-type phase and the β-Li<sub>3</sub>PS<sub>4</sub>-type phase, respectively. <sup>14,15</sup> On the other hand, the sample with  $0.67 \le k \le 0.72$  showed diffraction peaks from a small amount of impurity phases, and the samples with k = 0.73 and 0.74 were found to be mono-phasic in character. Fig. 4(b) shows the lattice parameters and volume of the  $Li_{4-k}Sn_{1-k}P_kS_4$  phase obtained in the present study. The lattice parameters decreased from k = 0.67 to 0.75, indicating the formation of the solid solution. The decrease in the lattice parameter is due to a decrease in the amount of  $\operatorname{Sn}^{4+}$  ions that have a larger ionic radius (r = 0.55 Å)than the  $P^{5+}$  ion (r = 0.17 Å), and also due to a decrease in the lithium content in the structure.

structure.title: Solid solutions of the LGPS-type phases
structure.text:
LGPS-type phases were synthesized in the Si (ref. 5, present study), Ge (ref. 12), and Sn (ref. 4, present study) systems, and all the LGPS-type phases form a solid solution with the composition  $\text{Li}_{4-k}M_{1-k}P_kS_4$  (M=Si,Ge,Sn). Fig. 5(a) summarizes the lattice volume data of the LGPS-type solid solutions as a function of k. Each system has a different range of the solid solutions:  $0.525 \le k \le 0.60$ ,  $0.50 \le k$  $\leq$  0.67, and 0.67  $\leq$   $k \leq$  0.75 in Li<sub>4-k</sub> $M_{1-k}P_kS_4$  for the Si, Ge, and Sn systems,

![](page_6_Figure_3.jpeg)

Fig. 4 (a) XRD patterns (left) and peak shifts (right) for the sample,  $\text{Li}_{4-k}\text{Sn}_{1-k}P_kS_4$  (0.50  $\leq k \leq$  0.75). (b) Composition dependence of the lattice parameters in the LGPS-type phase as a function of k in  $\text{Li}_{4-k}\text{Sn}_{1-k}P_kS_4$ .

respectively. The differences in the single-phase region are discussed below in relation to the size of the cations ( $\mathrm{Si}^{4+}$ ,  $\mathrm{Ge}^{4+}$ , and  $\mathrm{Sn}^{4+}$ ), which are present in the tetrahedral unit, ( $M/\mathrm{P}$ )S<sub>4</sub> on the 4d sites. Fig. 5(b) shows the volume of the ( $M/\mathrm{P}$ )S<sub>4</sub> unit as a function of the lattice volume together with other polyhedral units consisting of the framework structure, LiS<sub>6</sub> octahedra, and PS<sub>4</sub> tetrahedra. The volume of the ( $M/\mathrm{P}$ )S<sub>4</sub> unit became larger depending on the cation size in the order of  $M=\mathrm{Si}^{4+}$ ,  $\mathrm{Ge}^{4+}$ , and  $\mathrm{Sn}^{4+}$ . This indicates that the M ions occupy the ( $M/\mathrm{P}$ )S<sub>4</sub> tetrahedra. In contrast to the case of the ( $M/\mathrm{P}$ )S<sub>4</sub> unit, no significant volume changes were observed for the PS<sub>4</sub> tetrahedra, which connect four LiS<sub>6</sub> octahedra in the one-dimensional framework chain by sharing S(1) as shown in Fig. 6(a). This is consistent with the structure analysis results that no metal ions are situated at the P (2b) sites. The dependence on the size of the  $M^{4+}$  ions was also observed in the volume of the LiS<sub>6</sub> unit. The volume of the octahedra is affected by the size of the ( $M/\mathrm{P}$ )S<sub>4</sub> tetrahedra, because the octahedra share their S(2)–S(2) and S(3)–S(3) edges with the ( $M/\mathrm{P}$ )S<sub>4</sub> tetrahedra.

Fig. 6(b) shows the atomic distances between sulphide atoms at LiS<sub>6</sub> octahedra as a function of k in Li<sub>4-k</sub> $M_{1-<math>k$ </sub>P<sub>k</sub>S<sub>4</sub> (M = Si, Ge, Sn). The S(1)-S(1) distance was maintained constant with the variation of M and k, because no changes in the volume were observed for the PS<sub>4</sub> unit, which connects LiS<sub>6</sub> octahedra by sharing S(1). On the other hand, the S(2)-S(2) and S(3)-S(3) distances of all samples changed in the range of 3.47-3.70 and 3.35-3.63 Å, respectively. The ranges of the distances might be related to the composition range of the solid solution; the

![](page_7_Figure_3.jpeg)

Fig. 5 (a) Composition dependence of the lattice volume in monophasic of LGPS-type phase with k in  $\text{Li}_{4-k} P_k S_4$  (M = Si, Ge, Sn). (b) Variation in polyhedral volumes of monophasic LGPS-type phase as a function of lattice volume V. The values were calculated based on Rietveld analysis of synchrotron X-ray diffraction data for M = Si and Sn. For M = Ge, the values were calculated based on a previous study.<sup>12</sup>

smallest and largest values of the S–S bond distances correspond to the limit of the solid solution.

The compositions of the mono-phasic region shift to larger k values in the order of  $\mathrm{Si}^{4+}$ ,  $\mathrm{Ge}^{4+}$ ,  $\mathrm{Sn}^{4+}$ , which corresponds to the change in the ionic radius of  $\mathrm{Si}^{4+} < \mathrm{Ge}^{4+} < \mathrm{Sn}^{4+}$ . The single-phase region in the Si system ranges from k=0.525 to k=0.60, while the region in the Ge system expands to k=0.67. The monophasic region in the Sn system shifts to a higher k range compared to the Ge and Si systems.

nodes.text: Fig. 5(b) shows the volume of the ( $M/\mathrm{P}$ )S<sub>4</sub> unit as a function of the lattice volume together with other polyhedral units consisting of the framework structure, LiS<sub>6</sub> octahedra, and PS<sub>4</sub> tetrahedra. This indicates that the M ions occupy the ( $M/\mathrm{P}$ )S<sub>4</sub> tetrahedra. This is consistent with the structure analysis results that no metal ions are situated at the P (2b) sites.

structure.title: **Electrochemical properties**
structure.text:
The electrochemical stability of the solid electrolytes synthesized in the present study was measured by cyclic voltammetry using Li and Au as electrodes. Fig. 7(a) shows the cyclic voltammograms of solid electrolytes with compositions of  $\text{Li}_{3.45}\text{Si}_{0.45}\text{P}_{0.55}\text{S}_4$  (k=0.55 in  $\text{Li}_{4-k}\text{Si}_{1-k}\text{P}_k\text{S}_4$ ) and  $\text{Li}_{3.27}\text{Sn}_{0.27}\text{P}_{0.73}\text{S}_4$  (k=0.73 in  $\text{Li}_{4-k}\text{Sn}_{1-k}\text{P}_k\text{S}_4$ ). For both electrolytes, oxidization and reduction peaks are observed near 0 V  $\nu$ s.  $\text{Li}^+/\text{Li}$ . On the other hand, no significant reactions were observed up to 5 V  $\nu$ s.  $\text{Li}^+/\text{Li}$ . These results indicate that both electrolytes have a wide electrochemical window.

Ionic conductivity was measured by the ac impedance method over the temperature range of 253 K  $\leq$   $T \leq$  373 K with applied frequencies in the range between 100 Hz and 15 MHz. The conductivity values were determined from impedance plots of the data.

![](page_8_Figure_3.jpeg)

Fig. 6 (a) Coordination of sulphide atoms at LiS<sub>6</sub> octahedra. The large blue sphere represents Li(2), which is situated in the LiS<sub>6</sub> octahedra. Small spheres represent sulphide atoms. White spheres: S(1); grey spheres: S(2); black spheres: S(3). (b) Composition dependence of distances between sulphide atoms in the LiS<sub>6</sub> unit of the LGPS-type phase as a function of k in  $\text{Li}_{4-k}M_{1-k}P_kS_4$ . The values were calculated based on Rietveld analysis of synchrotron X-ray diffraction data for M = Si and Sn. For M = Ge, the values were calculated based on a previous study.12

Fig. 7(b) shows the impedance and Arrhenius plots of Li<sub>3.45</sub>Si<sub>0.45</sub>P<sub>0.55</sub>S<sub>4</sub>  $(k = 0.55 \text{ in } \text{Li}_{4-k}\text{Si}_{1-k}\text{P}_k\text{S}_4)$ . The impedance plots consist of a semicircle and a spike, which respectively correspond to contributions from the bulk/grain boundary and the electrode. The total conductivity at each temperature was

![](page_8_Figure_6.jpeg)

Fig. 7 (a) Cyclic voltammograms for LGPS type phases, Li<sub>3.45</sub>Si<sub>0.45</sub>P<sub>0.55</sub>S<sub>4</sub> (upper) and Li<sub>3.27</sub>Sn<sub>0.27</sub>P<sub>0.73</sub>S<sub>4</sub> (lower). (b) Arrhenius plots and cole-cole plots for Li<sub>3.45</sub>Si<sub>0.45</sub>P<sub>0.55</sub>S<sub>4</sub>.

obtained as a sum of the bulk and grain boundary resistances. The activation energy for ionic conduction was calculated to be 0.27 eV, which is a typical value for superionic conductors. The total conductivity value of 6.7  $\times$ 10<sup>-3</sup> S cm<sup>-1</sup> at room temperature was slightly lower than that of the Ge system, LGPS  $(1.2 \times 10^{-2} \text{ S cm}^{-1})$ , and was higher than that of  $\text{Li}_{3.4}\text{Si}_{0.4}\text{P}_{0.6}\text{S}_4$  with the thio-LISICON phase  $(6.4 \times 10^{-4} \text{ S cm}^{-1})$ . Although these two compositions are close to each other (Li<sub>3.45</sub>Si<sub>0.45</sub>P<sub>0.55</sub>S<sub>4</sub> with the LGPS-type and Li<sub>3.4</sub>Si<sub>0.4</sub>P<sub>0.6</sub>S<sub>4</sub> with the thio-LISICON-type), the LGPS structure provided higher lithium ionic conduction.

Fig. 8(a) shows the total ionic conductivities at room temperature for the mono-phasic composition ranges for all the LGPS-type phases as a function of k in  $\text{Li}_{4-k}M_{1-k}P_kS_4$  (M = Si, Ge, Sn). For the Si system, the maximum conductivity was obtained at k = 0.55, smaller than that observed for the Ge system at k = 0.55. For M = Sn, the conductivity of the sample with k = 0.67 (the nominal composition of Li<sub>10</sub>SnP<sub>2</sub>S<sub>12</sub>, which is out of the solid-solution range) was close to the reported values  $(3.7 \times 10^{-3} \text{ S cm}^{-1} \text{ in this study and } 4.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ S cm}^{-1} \text{ in a previous})$ study<sup>4</sup>). However, the maximum value of  $5.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ S cm}^{-1}$  was obtained at k = 0.73, which indicates that the single-phase of the LGPS-type has higher conductivity. Fig. 8(b) illustrates the relationships between the ionic conductivity, lattice volume, and composition parameter k in  $\text{Li}_{4-k}M_{1-k}P_kS_4$  (M = Si, Ge, Sn). The lattice volume plays a key role for the Si and Ge systems; the compositions of the larger volume show higher ionic conductivity values. On the other hand, the kvalue also affects ionic conductivity for the Sn system. Although a large lattice volume was obtained for the Sn system, lower ionic conductivity was observed. This can be explained by larger k values of  $\text{Li}_{4-k}M_{1-k}P_kS_4$  for the Sn system, which corresponds to smaller amounts of Li ions in the unit cell. Low concentration of lithium for conduction might result in lower ionic conductivity compared to the Si and Ge systems.

![](page_9_Figure_5.jpeg)

Fig. 8 (a) Composition dependence of the ionic conductivity at room temperature in the LGPS-type phase with k in Li<sub>4-k</sub> $M_{1-k}P_kS_4$  (M = Si, Ge, and Sn). (b) The relationships between ionic conductivity, lattice volume and composition parameter in monophasic LGPS-type phases. For germanium related systems (M = Ge; M = Ge, Si; M = Ge, Sn), the values are cited from previous studies. 12,16

The ionic conductivity of the LGPS-type phase might be understood by the lattice volume and the lithium concentration that participates in the ionic conduction.

- (i) A large lattice volume yields high ionic conductivity. To increase the lattice volume, the choice of the M atoms is important. The M atoms situate in the (M/P)  $S_4$  tetrahedra which form a one-dimensional framework chain and this expands the cell volume according to the ionic radii:  $Si^{4+} < Ge^{4+} < Sn^{4+}$ .
- (ii) The change in the lattice volume is related to the structure restriction. The change in the size of the one-dimensional framework polyhedra (LiS<sub>6</sub> octahedra and  $(M/P)S_4$  tetrahedra) might be restricted by the S(2)-S(2) and S(3)-S(3) distances, which were found to determine the single phase region.
- (iii) As the aliovalent M cation changes the lithium composition, the lithium concentration that participates in the ionic conduction is determined by the higher and lower limits of the lattice volume. Therefore, the range of the solid solution changed with the lattice volume;  $0.525 \le k \le 0.60$  for M = Si,  $0.50 \le k \le 0.67$  for M = Ge, and  $0.67 \le k \le 0.75$  for M = Sn in the composition,  $\text{Li}_{4-k}M_{1-k}P_kS_4$  (M = Si, Ge, Sn). Since the lithium concentration in the Sn system is lower than in the other two systems, the conductivity of the Sn system is lower than those of the Ge and Si systems.

nodes.title: Compositional Dependence of Ionic Conductivity and Lattice Volume
nodes.text:
Fig. 8(a) shows the total ionic conductivities at room temperature for the mono-phasic composition ranges for all the LGPS-type phases as a function of k in  $\text{Li}_{4-k}M_{1-k}P_kS_4$  (M = Si, Ge, Sn). For the Si system, the maximum conductivity was obtained at k = 0.55, smaller than that observed for the Ge system at k = 0.55. For M = Sn, the conductivity of the sample with k = 0.67 (the nominal composition of Li<sub>10</sub>SnP<sub>2</sub>S<sub>12</sub>, which is out of the solid-solution range) was close to the reported values  $(3.7 \times 10^{-3} \text{ S cm}^{-1} \text{ in this study and } 4.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ S cm}^{-1} \text{ in a previous})$ study<sup>4</sup>). However, the maximum value of  $5.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ S cm}^{-1}$  was obtained at k = 0.73, which indicates that the single-phase of the LGPS-type has higher conductivity. Fig. 8(b) illustrates the relationships between the ionic conductivity, lattice volume, and composition parameter k in  $\text{Li}_{4-k}M_{1-k}P_kS_4$  (M = Si, Ge, Sn). The lattice volume plays a key role for the Si and Ge systems; the compositions of the larger volume show higher ionic conductivity values. On the other hand, the kvalue also affects ionic conductivity for the Sn system. Although a large lattice volume was obtained for the Sn system, lower ionic conductivity was observed. nodes.title: Key Factors Influencing Ionic Conduction
nodes.text:
A large lattice volume yields high ionic conductivity. To increase the lattice volume, the choice of the M atoms is important. The M atoms situate in the (M/P)  $S_4$  tetrahedra which form a one-dimensional framework chain and this expands the cell volume according to the ionic radii:  $Si^{4+} < Ge^{4+} < Sn^{4+}$ . - (ii) The change in the lattice volume is related to the structure restriction. The change in the size of the one-dimensional framework polyhedra (LiS<sub>6</sub> octahedra and  $(M/P)S_4$  tetrahedra) might be restricted by the S(2)-S(2) and S(3)-S(3) distances, which were found to determine the single phase region.
- (iii) As the aliovalent M cation changes the lithium composition, the lithium concentration that participates in the ionic conduction is determined by the higher and lower limits of the lattice volume. Therefore, the range of the solid solution changed with the lattice volume;  $0.525 \le k \le 0.60$  for M = Si,  $0.50 \le k \le 0.67$  for M = Ge, and  $0.67 \le k \le 0.75$  for M = Sn in the composition,  $\text{Li}_{4-k}M_{1-k}P_kS_4$  (M = Si, Ge, Sn). Since the lithium concentration in the Sn system is lower than in the other two systems, the conductivity of the Sn system is lower than those of the Ge and Si systems.

nodes.title: Since the lithium concentration in the S...
nodes.text: Since the lithium concentration in the Sn system is lower than in the other two systems, the conductivity of the Sn system is lower than those of the Ge and Si systems.

structure.title: Conclusion
structure.text: The solid solutions of LGPS-type phases have been investigated for the composition of  $\text{Li}_{4-k}M_{1-k}P_kS_4$  with M=Si, Ge, and Sn. The LGPS-type phase of the Si system was successfully synthesized by a solid-state reaction in an evacuated sealed tube. All the systems showed a certain range of solid solution, and the composition range in each system depended on the ionic radii of the substituted cation  $(M^{4+})$ . The ionic conductivity changed with the size of the M cations and Li compositions. Although the highest ionic conduction was proposed by first principle calculation, the Si system showed lower ionic conductivity than the Ge system.
